title: Our own bottom
hookLine: on the highest throne in the world, we still sit on our own bottom (Essays 3.13)
last: BE WHOLLY IN WHAT YOU DO; DRIFT, RETURN.

lines: A KING CLIMBS TO HIS THRONE.
ON THE THRONE, OUR OWN BOTTOM.
cards: A king climbs the steps to his throne. Velvet, gold, a crowd holding its breath. He turns, gathers his robes, and sits down.
On what, exactly? Near the very end of Of experience, Montaigne answers with a joke. It's no use climbing up on stilts, he says, because on stilts we still have to walk with our own legs.
And on the highest throne in the world, we are still sitting on our own bottom.

teach.b: First, the joke. It's a little rude, and that's the point. A throne is the grandest seat there is, and the body on it is as ordinary as anyone's.
The laugh punctures the idea that rank, title or achievement lifts a person out of being human. Second, the stilts.
Stilts are anything we use to seem taller: a job title, a following, an expensive coat, being right in an argument. Fine, climb up.
You're still walking on your own legs, with their aches and limits. Nothing you stand on changes what you're standing with.

Third, angels and beasts. In the same closing pages he warns about people who want to rise above the human, to escape being a person altogether. Instead of turning into angels, he says, they turn into beasts.
He's wary of any striving, however lofty, that despises the body and ordinary life.
Readers differ on how far to take this: some hear a gentle check on pride, others a reminder that the spiritual life is lived in a body, at a table, among people.

Not with contempt; with relief. The pressure to be more than human is heavy, and Montaigne sets it down with one cheerful, slightly rude sentence. Whether you feel very important or very small, the line works both ways.
Everyone you meet is sitting on the same thing.

how: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that even on the highest throne we sit on our own bottom as a cheerful check on pride and a reminder that every life is lived in an ordinary body.

o: a royal custom of bowing low before the throne
the lowest seat at a feast, kept for the humble
a reminder that no throne lifts anyone out of being human

games.q: the end of Of experience: tap the pairs.
p: still walking on our own legs

s: Montaigne says a high enough throne lifts a ruler above ordinary life
on the highest throne in the world, he says, we still sit on our own bottom.
he warns that those who try to become angels turn into beasts
he is wary of striving that despises the body and ordinary life.
he says stilts let us walk without our own legs
on stilts we still walk with our own legs.

games.q: you've just been handed a grand title and a seat at the head of the table. what does Montaigne remind you?
o: you're now more than other people.
you're still sitting on your own bottom.
games.why: he doesn't say refuse the seat. he says no throne, however high, lifts you out of being human, and he says it with a laugh.

practice: Feel what you're sitting on: the chair, the floor, your own weight settling down.

Bring to mind something you've been taking very seriously about yourself, a title, a reputation, a plan that has to go perfectly, and set it beside the plain fact of sitting here in a body, like everyone else.
Notice whether it weighs a little less.

wordCard.voice: Our own bottom. Montaigne's cheerful reminder that no throne lifts anyone out of being human. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my own bottom. Same seat as everyone, king or not. See you tomorrow.
